highlight.title: Declining Occupations and Career Outcomes in Norway
highlight.summary: NBER working paper by Barth, Hoen, Kerr, and Kerr examines career consequences for workers initially employed in occupations that subsequently decline by at least 25% during 2007–2024 in Norway. Workers in declining occupations face measurable long-term wage and employment penalties, offering cross-national evidence on the structural costs of occupational displacement. The findings are broadly applicable to understanding white-collar and professional displacement dynamics driven by automation and AI.

extractedStats.overlayLabel: Workers in occupations declining 25%+ lose 0.4 years of work in Norway 2007–2024
extractedStats.quote: Workers initially employed in occupations that later decline by at least 25% demonstrate 0.4 lower future years of work, although this employment difference is mostly explained by other individual traits.

extractedStats.overlayLabel: Workers in declining occupations face 4.7% cumulative earnings loss vs. starting earnings
extractedStats.quote: These workers, conditional on controls, experience a 4.7% reduction in future cumulative earnings relative to starting earnings, akin to losing one year's worth of earnings over 2007–2024.

highlight.title: Shaping Human Capital and Work Practices in a Changing Labor Market
highlight.summary: Wittich (2026) explores how human capital formation and workplace practices are adapting amid rapid labor market transformation driven by technological change, including AI adoption. The paper considers how workers and firms update skills and routines in response to automation pressures. It provides a conceptual framework relevant to forecasting overall US displacement trajectories.

highlight.title: The Relic Condition: When Published Scholarship Becomes Material for Its Own Replacement
highlight.summary: Deng and Liu (2026) demonstrate that LLMs can replicate the scholarly reasoning systems of prominent humanities and social science researchers by extracting structured inference constraints from their published corpora alone, then deploying these as 'scholar-bots.' The study raises urgent questions about AI substitution of high-skill knowledge workers in academic and creative domains. This work has direct implications for creative and knowledge-industry displacement forecasts.

highlight.title: Reckoning with the Political Economy of AI: Avoiding Decoys in Pursuit of Accountability
highlight.summary: Vertesi, boyd, Taylor, and Shestakofsky (2026) argue that AI development is a world-building endeavor through which funders and developers entrench networks of power and wealth, often deploying accountability 'decoys' that deflect meaningful oversight. The paper situates AI's labor market impacts within a broader political economy, warning that structural workforce transformations may be obscured by superficial governance gestures. This framing is highly relevant to tracking AI adoption rates and their workforce exposure effects.

highlight.title: Why Open Source? A Game-Theoretic Analysis of the AI Race
highlight.summary: Mladenovic, Courville, and Gidel (2026) model open-sourcing versus closed-sourcing decisions among frontier AI developers using an R&D race framework, finding that competitive dynamics systematically shape which capabilities become widely available. Broad diffusion of open-source AI models accelerates enterprise adoption and, by extension, workforce exposure to AI-driven automation. The paper's findings are directly relevant to projecting the pace of AI adoption across the economy.
